label: Keeping a place in the text
objective: Use details from the passage to answer questions about Tim and his ball.
report: During a short reading task, the learner twice returned to a line they had already read. When the teacher put two sentences on each strip, the learner moved through the strips in order. The learner answered the teacher’s questions by pointing to details in the story.

observations.finding: On two occasions, the learner returned to a line already read.
observations.quote: the learner twice returned to a line they had already read.

observations.finding: The learner followed the text in order when it was presented in two-sentence strips.
observations.quote: When the teacher put two sentences on each strip, the learner moved through the strips in order.

profile.support: Keep the original words. Group each pair of sentences in a separate block so the learner can mark their place.

reading_blocks: A boy called Tim has a red ball. He takes it to the park.
His dog comes with him. The dog runs after a bird.
The ball goes under the big oak tree. Tim looks for the ball.
He looks and he looks. Then he sees a hole near the tree.
Tim puts his hand into the hole. The ball is in the hole.
He takes the ball out. He kicks the ball to the dog.
The dog is happy now. Tim is happy too.
His mother waits at the gate. The sun is warm today.
worksheet.support_activity: Use a finger or a strip of paper to mark the block you are reading. Start with the first block. When you reach “park,” move your marker to the next block. Keep going one block at a time.

questions.question: Where does Tim take his ball?
questions.answer: He takes it to the park.
questions.evidence: A boy called Tim has a red ball. He takes it to the park.

questions.question: Where does Tim find the ball?
questions.answer: In a hole near the tree.
questions.evidence: Then he sees a hole near the tree. Tim puts his hand into the hole. The ball is in the hole.

questions.question: What does Tim do with the ball just after he takes it out?
questions.answer: He kicks it to the dog.
questions.evidence: He takes the ball out. He kicks the ball to the dog.

worksheet.teacher_note: The eight blocks use the original words in their original order. Invite the learner to move their marker independently, then return to a block to show the detail that supports each answer.

label: Working out who “he” means
objective: Use details from the passage to answer questions about Tim and his ball.
report: In a story about a boy and his dog, the learner could name both characters. When the next sentence began with “he,” the learner pointed to the dog as the person doing the action. After the teacher asked, “Whose name could go there?”, the learner looked back and pointed to the boy’s name.

observations.finding: The learner named the characters but attached “he” to the wrong character in the following sentence.
observations.quote: When the next sentence began with “he,” the learner pointed to the dog as the person doing the action.

observations.finding: A prompt to replace the pronoun with a name led the learner to look back at the text.
observations.quote: After the teacher asked, “Whose name could go there?”, the learner looked back and pointed to the boy’s name.

profile.support: Model replacing “he” with “Tim” once. Keep a later example of “he” for the learner to resolve by looking back.

reading_blocks: A boy called Tim has a red ball. Tim takes the ball to the park. His dog comes with him. The dog runs after a bird.
The ball goes under the big oak tree. Tim looks for the ball. He looks and he looks. Then he sees a hole near the tree.
Tim puts his hand into the hole. The ball is in the hole. Tim takes the ball out. He kicks the ball to the dog.
The dog is happy now. Tim is happy too. His mother waits at the gate. The sun is warm today.
worksheet.support_activity: In the original story, “He takes it to the park” means “Tim takes the ball to the park.” Now find “He kicks the ball to the dog.” Look at the sentence just before it. Point to the name that could replace “He.” Read the kicking sentence aloud using the name.

questions.answer: He kicks it to the dog.

worksheet.teacher_note: The opening names Tim and the ball explicitly. The kicking sentence keeps the pronoun so the learner can use the previous sentence to identify Tim. For the last question, invite the learner to show both the name and the action.
